items.title: 2.2.3 Intersection of a Linear Function and a Quadratic Function

blocks.text: A line and a parabola can either intersect at two points, one point or not intersect at all. If there are two solutions, the system has two points of intersection. A single solution indicates that there is only one intersection point, suggesting that the line may be tangent to the parabola. If no solution exists, it means the line and the parabola do not intersect.

blocks.alt: Three panels, each with x and y axes and an upward parabola. Two Solutions: a line cuts the parabola at two dots. One Solution: a line touches the parabola at one dot. No Solutions: a line passes the parabola without meeting it.
blocks.caption: Figure: a line and a parabola with two, one or no points of intersection (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: The three panels of the figure are labelled "Two Solutions", "One Solutions" and "No Solutions".

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels the middle panel "One Solutions". With one point it should read "One Solution" (singular), as in our figure.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quadratic function \(y = ax^{2} + bx + c\) (\(a \ne 0\)) has a U-shaped graph called a parabola: it opens upward when \(a > 0\) and downward when \(a < 0\). Its turning point is the vertex, at \(x = -\frac{b}{2a}\).
A tangent is a line that just touches a curve at one point without crossing it there.
Why only 0, 1 or 2 points? Putting the line's \(y\) into the parabola's equation gives a quadratic equation in \(x\). A quadratic equation has two, one (repeated) or no real roots, according to its discriminant \(b^{2} - 4ac\) being positive, zero or negative.

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.problem: Solve the linear function \(y = -x + 3\) and quadratic function \(y = x^{2} - 6x + 3\) graphically.
steps:
Given: the linear function \(y = -x + 3\) and the quadratic function \(y = x^{2} - 6x + 3\).
To find: the points where their graphs meet (the solutions of the system).
Method: draw both graphs on the same axes and read the meeting points (the book's method). For the line we need its two intercepts; for the parabola we need its intercepts and its vertex (the turning point).

Step 1: Intercepts of the line \(y = -x + 3\)
\[x = 0:\ y = 3\]
\[y = 0:\ 0 = -x + 3 \Rightarrow x = 3\]
So the line passes through \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\).
Why: two points are enough to draw a straight line, and the intercepts are the easiest two.

Step 2: \(y\)-intercept of the parabola
\[y = x^{2} - 6x + 3 \quad \text{...(i)}\]
Put \(x = 0\) in (i): \(y = 3\), so \((0, 3)\) is the \(y\)-intercept.
Why: on the \(y\)-axis \(x = 0\).

Step 3: \(x\)-intercepts of the parabola
Put \(y = 0\) in (i):
\[0 = x^{2} - 6x + 3\]
Use the quadratic formula with \(a = 1, b = -6, c = 3\):
\[x = \dfrac{-(-6) \pm \sqrt{(-6)^{2} - 4(1)(3)}}{2(1)}\]
\[x = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 12}}{2}\]
\[x = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{24}}{2}\]
Why: \(x^{2} - 6x + 3\) does not factorise with whole numbers, so the quadratic formula \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a}\) is used.

Step 4: Simplify the roots
\[\sqrt{24} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = 2\sqrt{6}\]
\[x = \dfrac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{6}\]
\[x = 3 - \sqrt{6},\ 3 + \sqrt{6}\]
\[x \approx 0.6,\ 5.4\]
So \((0.6, 0)\) and \((5.4, 0)\) are the \(x\)-intercepts.
Why: \(\sqrt{6} \approx 2.449\), so \(3 - 2.449 \approx 0.55 \approx 0.6\) and \(3 + 2.449 \approx 5.45 \approx 5.4\) (to one decimal place, as the book gives them).

Step 5: The vertex \((h, k)\) of the parabola
\[h = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{-6}{2(1)} = 3\]
\[k = (3)^{2} - 6(3) + 3\]
\[k = 9 - 18 + 3 = -6\]
So the vertex is \((3, -6)\).
Why: the vertex is the lowest point of this parabola (\(a = 1 > 0\), so it opens upward); its \(x\)-coordinate is \(-\frac{b}{2a}\), and \(k\) is the value of the function there.

Step 6: Draw both graphs and read the meeting points
Draw the line through \((0, 3)\) and \((3, 0)\), and the parabola through \((0.6, 0)\), \((3, -6)\), \((5.4, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\) (see the graph below). They meet at \((0, 3)\) and \((5, -2)\).
Why: a point common to both graphs satisfies both equations, so it is a solution.

Check:
Put the two expressions for \(y\) equal:
\[x^{2} - 6x + 3 = -x + 3\]
\[x^{2} - 5x = 0\]
\[x(x - 5) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 \text{ or } x = 5\]
\(x = 0\): \(y = -0 + 3 = 3\); \(x = 5\): \(y = -5 + 3 = -2\).
Also \(5^{2} - 6(5) + 3 = 25 - 30 + 3 = -2\). Both points are correct.
blocks.answer: The solutions (points of intersection) are \((0, 3)\) and \((5, -2)\).

blocks.alt: Graph of the line y = minus x + 3 and the parabola y = x squared minus 6x + 3 on a grid, x from minus 2 to 7 and y from minus 7 to 6. Dots mark (0, 3) and (5, minus 2), where they meet, the vertex (3, minus 6) and the parabola's x-intercepts near 0.6 and 5.4.
blocks.caption: Figure: y = −x + 3 and y = x² − 6x + 3 meet at (0, 3) and (5, −2) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's graph prints the \(x\)-axis numbers \(-2\) and \(-1\) and the \(y\)-axis number \(-2\) without their minus signs. They lie on the negative side of the axes, so they are \(-2\), \(-1\) and \(-2\), as in our figure.
Hence \((0, 3)\) and \((5, -2)\) are the solutions (points of intersection) of the given functions.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A line and a parabola meet in two points, one point (the line is a tangent) or no point.
2. To draw a parabola: \(y\)-intercept (\(x = 0\)), \(x\)-intercepts (\(y = 0\), quadratic formula) and vertex \(h = -\frac{b}{2a}\), \(k = f(h)\).
3. Read the meeting points from the graph, then check by solving the two equations together.
4. The number of meeting points matches the number of real roots of the combined quadratic equation.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Sign errors in the quadratic formula: \(-b = -(-6) = 6\) and \((-6)^{2} = 36\).
2. Forgetting to simplify \(\sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}\) and to divide every term by 2: \(\frac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{6}\).
3. Confusing the \(x\)-intercepts of the parabola with the points of intersection: the answers are the points common to both graphs, \((0, 3)\) and \((5, -2)\).
4. Drawing the parabola with a pointed bottom: it is a smooth curve, rounded at the vertex.
